body_markdown:
With the much-anticipated (and many times delayed) Tesla Roadster finally debuting today, there’s a new kid on the EV sports car block. It’s not a very large or heavily populated block. It’s certainly not a cheap block, either. But if we turn back the clock almost 20 years, there weren’t *any* electric sports cars on the market. Electric drivetrains of any kind were the stuff of golf carts and dreary European city boxes.


The[Tesla Roadster](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/teslas-roadster-turns-10/) , the original one, was therefore a big deal when it arrived (also, funny enough, after multiple delays) in 2008. It wasn’t just the first series-production automobile to use lithium-ion batteries for motivation. It was also the very first model from what would become the world’s most valuable carmaker (by market cap, anyway), and a car that helped shift EVs into the mainstream. It was the first electric production car in living memory that anyone would really consider “cool.” All these years later, and with the new Roadster on the horizon, how does the market treat the groundbreaking original in collector car terms?


Getty Images/Rick Eglinton/Toronto Star


In 2003, Tesla was just another upstart California firm, named after a kooky long-dead Serbian-American inventor. But in true 2000s tech company fashion, things moved fast. By ’04, they had a fresh injection of funding from Elon Musk, flush with PayPal dollars and soon to be chairman at the carmaker. Tesla quickly went through multiple rounds of multi-million-dollar fundraising and had a coherent business plan: Start with a low-volume, premium electric sports car, and then expand into mainstream segments.


Designing an automobile from scratch, however, is what engineers describe as “difficult.” Doing it quickly, and doing it as a brand new company with no experience, makes it even more so. Tesla *did* have cutting-edge battery tech in the form of lithium-ion battery cells, which were lighter, more efficient, and punchier in an automotive application than the[lead-acid batteries in EVs of old](https://www.hagerty.com/media/member-stories/my-vw-elektro-bus-was-the-predecessor-to-the-id-buzz/) . They just didn’t have a car to put them in.


So the Tesla folks took a shortcut, looking across the Atlantic to Lotus. Specifically, the brilliant extruded- and bonded-aluminum chassis used in the[Elise](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h0jXhOmL7Xg&pp=ygUTbG90dXMgZWxpc2UgY2FtbWlzYQ%3D%3D) . It was a proven, lightweight, durable platform, and Lotus already had experience modifying it for other manufacturers with GM Europe’s Vauxhall VX220/Opel Speedster twins. Tesla finalized a contract with Lotus in July 2005 that called for 2500 gliders (completed cars minus powertrain) built in the U.K. then shipped to California for final assembly and distribution. Compared to the original, Toyota-powered Lotus product, the Tesla had its wheelbase extended by 2 inches.


The chassis was also strengthened and modified to accommodate the dimensions and torque of the electric powertrain, and the body made of carbon fiber to offset some of that powertrain’s considerable heft. Brakes were enlarged, and wheels changed from a four- to five-lug pattern. Styling and interior changes were major, though the Elise family resemblance is definitely there. Still, Tesla claims only 6–7% parts sharing with the Lotus.


Tesla eagerly announced the model in 2006 and had prototypes on the road the same year, but there were multiple delays, and many of them came down to the transmission. A two-speed unit was in the plans and multiple designs were tested, but ultimately a more durable single-speed unit from BorgWarner won out.


Matt Tierney


The production version was ready in 2008. The star of the show, of course, was the then-novel means of propulsion. It consisted of 6831 lithium-ion cells, with 69 cells making up a brick, nine bricks making up a sheet, and 11 sheets in series making up the complete battery. Tesla claimed 10-fold fewer CO2 emissions than that of comparable gas-powered cars and a range of 244 miles. But this was a sports car, and sports car people are concerned with different sorts of numbers.


Horsepower came in at 248 and torque at 273 lb-ft. Nothing crazy even in 2008, but the way the Tesla delivered that instant, shot-out-of-a-cannon feeling made an impression. “Squeeze the throttle, and the Tesla surges forward with relative ease,” according to *Car and Driver* . “There’s no wheelspin, axle tramp, shutter, jutter, smoke whiff, cowl shake, nothing” said *Motor Trend* . “I’m being eerily teleported down the barrel of a rail gun, head pulled back by a hard, steady acceleration. Bizarre.”


Getting to 60 mph took about four seconds, though the Roadster topped out at 125. Another number sports car people care about is price, and the Roadster started at about $100K. That wasn’t obscene given what it was capable of and the still-small company it came from, but it was still over twice as expensive as an Elise.


Matt Tierney


Broad Arrow


Tesla made its first profit in July 2009, when it delivered 109 vehicles. (How quaint. It delivered nearly half a million vehicles in Q3 2026). In 2010, Roadsters got an improved interior, including a push-button gear selection that replaced the previous aluminum knob, better HVAC, and more sound deadening. Later the same year, a “Roadster 2.5” update included different wheels and seats as well as an optional 7-inch touchscreen with reversing camera. Tesla also introduced the “Roadster Sport,” with a higher-output motor (288 hp and 295 lb-ft) that dropped the 0-60 time to 3.7 seconds and raised the price by $20K, but kept the same 125-mph top speed and 244 miles of range.


Roadster production was all done by early 2012. The contract with Lotus was fulfilled with 2450 cars built, and a federal noncompliant airbag exemption (which also applied to the Elise) expired. Tesla’s first mainstream product—the Model S—started rolling off the lines a few months later, and the rest is history. The company did offer an upgrade to existing cars a few years later, in 2015–16. Called the “Roadster 3.0” and priced at $29,000, it installed a higher-capacity battery pack along with an aero kit and tires with lower rolling resistance. It’s unclear how many owners went for it. Then, in 2018, SpaceX strapped Musk’s 2010 Roadster to a rocket and launched it into space, making it the first production car to reach the final frontier.


James Lipman


A few years ago, we had about six hours behind the wheel of a Roadster. Driving one of these early adopter Teslas is a unique experience, though comparisons to its hydrocarbon-burning British cousin are tough not to make. First off, it’s carrying a lot more mass, about 1000 pounds more (roughly 1900 for the Lotus, 2900 for the Tesla), and it’s obvious from the first time it changes direction. It’s more reluctant to do so, and the unassisted steering is heavier at low speeds. It just doesn’t feel as light on its feet, because it really isn’t.


But that’s compared with a Lotus. Compared to almost anything else, it enjoys sharp turn-in and neutral, balanced cornering with a low center of gravity, though the Tesla does carry slightly more of its weight at the rear than the Lotus does. The bigger differences come with the pedal on the right. When you press it, there’s instant takeoff and uninterrupted acceleration, with little noise other than a mild electric whine, and wind. It’s not as neck-snapping as, say, a Model S Plaid, but it’s much more thrust than an Elise. When you let go of that pedal, the Roadster goes into full regen mode to claw back some of the juice you just spent gunning it. Overall, it’s a nice combination of digital heart in an analog body, and as a result feels more connected and engaging than other EVs.


Matt Tierney


Matt Tierney


Matt Tierney


Matt Tierney


On a sunny day with the top off and some curvy pavement ahead, the Roadster is a nice place to be. It’s easy to drive. It’s thrilling when you want it to be. It’s otherwise undramatic. That said, a certain type of driver, on a certain type of road, might get over the novelty of effortless EV acceleration before too long. They might miss the zing of an eager twin-cam four, and the self-satisfaction that comes with heel-toe downshifting and push-pulling on a little aluminum ball.


Living with an early Roadster, meanwhile, isn’t as straightforward as it is with a new Model 3. Roadsters charge through AC current only, so no fast charging and no plugging into Tesla’s Supercharger network, which means a full charge takes at least a few hours. Anything longer than a day trip really isn’t an option, then, and that 244 miles of range is a bit optimistic for the real world for anyone who drives this sports car like, well, a sports car.


Heat cycles, mileage, and the slow march of time also diminish battery capacity. If a battery pack needs replacing, the bill will be well into the thousands, though there are companies like[re/cell](https://recell-ev.com/tesla-roadster-1) in Texas that offer battery upgrades in addition to replacements. Other big pain points noted by owners on the Tesla forums are limited to the HVAC system and failure of the Power Electronics Module (PEM). Taking a Roadster to a Tesla service center isn’t always as easy as dropping the car off and handing over the keys, either, as availability of parts and qualified technicians for a model that’s been gone since 2012 is limited. There’s also little incentive for Tesla to give much support long-term, as *total* Roadster production from 2008–11 is less than *daily* Tesla production in 2026. There are at least some independent shops across the country that work on Roadsters, but there isn’t exactly one in every town.


The Roadster is nevertheless a smart-looking, quick, entertaining sports car with a high price tag and low production numbers. That’s the kind of stuff that usually adds up to a car becoming “collectible,” and that was our thinking in 2022 when we put the Roadster on our annual[Bull Market](https://www.hagerty.com/media/magazine-features/bull-market-2022/) list, which predicts cars that are poised to rise in value over the subsequent 12 months.


The Tesla was not our most prescient pick, at least long term. Values did rise a bit in 2022 before peaking in 2023, but the average condition #2 (excellent) value is down 35% since it went on the list, even though our other selections from that year are up 38%. Currently, #3 (good) values for a[Roadster](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=tesla+roadster) range from $50K to $60K, while #2 values run in the $70K to $80K range. Earlier this year, Roadster values were the lowest they’ve been since we started tracking them, but they recorded modest increases over the past two quarters.


Values for the[Lotus Elise](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=lotus+elise) , for reference, run in the mid-$30K range for #3 condition and the mid-$50K range for #2 condition. At least part of the difference comes down to scarcity, as Lotus sold over twice as many Elises in the U.S. as Tesla sold Roadsters worldwide.


The core audience for Roadsters is Gen Xers, who make up 42% of insurance quotes for the Tesla, compared to 30% for the Elise and 31% for the market as a whole. Millennials and baby boomers each make up 24% of quotes for the Tesla. Gen Zers quote just 6% of Roadsters, compared to 10% for the Elise and 10% for the market as a whole. The top states quoting Roadsters are the sunny climes of California, Texas, and Arizona.


Bring a Trailer/Prototype37


Nobody makes a sports car quite like the Elise anymore, and despite some of its futuristic features, nobody makes a sports car quite like the Roadster anymore, either. Even if Tesla went bankrupt tomorrow, the company’s place in car history is secure; and the Roadster is the car that started it all. Lessons learned and revenue earned from it pushed the company to new heights as the first major American carmaker to spring up in living memory.


A lot of people dislike Tesla as a company, and a lot of people dislike the boss. Plenty of car people also dislike EVs in general. So the original Roadster’s appeal is always going to be limited relative to something like a Corvette or a Mustang. But whatever you think of Tesla, Musk, or EVs, it’s a historically important vehicle and still very rewarding behind the wheel. To that end, it will always hold appeal for the kind of enthusiast that gets a jolt from just seeing it (plugged in) inside their garage.


[Stefan Lombard](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/stefan-lombard/)
